body.text: Nayib Bukele, a close Trump ally and president of El Salvador, recently announced that the country’s new 50,000-seat National Stadium, set to be “the largest and most modern in Central America,” is 75 percent complete. It is being financed and built by China.

This illustrates a broader regional trend. Across ideological lines, from De la Espriella’s Colombia and Milei’s Argentina all the way to Sheinbaum’s Mexico and the Ortegas’ Nicaragua, China remains the partner of choice for most Latin American states in key areas.

In Argentina, anarcho-capitalist and close Trump ally Javier Milei, who once vowed not to do business with “any communist,” in August extended his central bank’s $19 billion currency swap with the People’s Bank of China through to 2031, even after a Trump envoy called it “extortionate.” In Colombia, President Abelardo De la Espriella toured the Bogotá Metro, built by a consortium led by state-owned China Harbour Engineering, and pledged to back a second line for which a Chinese-led group is bidding. In Peru, Cosco’s Chancay port, which was developed by Cosco Shipping Ports Chancay Peru S.A., handled 200,000 TEUs in the first half of 2026, up 71 percent during the same period in 2025.

On top of this, Chinese firms have invested some $72 billion in the region’s mining sector since 2000, and energy giants State Grid Corporation of China and State Power Investment Corporation rank among its largest foreign investors. And at Expomin, Latin America’s largest mining expo, Chinese companies formed the biggest national contingent.

Despite American complaints and the U.S. openly using force to make itself the “partner of choice” in the region, these projects have continued. Can there really be any choice if there is overwhelming force involved? As it turns out, yes – and in key areas Latin American nations are still choosing China.

The U.S. approach has been to call Chinese investment projects “interference,” while itself actively promoting election meddling, regime change, and direct conflict, often purely for the purpose of extraction or muscle-flexing. This has not been received well in the region. The 2026 Latinobarómetro, reported by Al Jazeera, found that for the first time since 1995, Latin Americans view China’s influence more positively than America’s, 65 percent to 57, up from 48 percent for China in 2020. The gap is starkest among Washington’s closest partners: 72 percent of Salvadorans rate China’s influence positively, against 64 percent for the United States, while the U.S. trails by 18 points in Milei’s Argentina and 24 in Kast’s Chile. Region-wide, 55 percent expect Trump’s policies to harm the world; in Mexico, 79 percent do.

The Pew Research Center likewise found views of the United States worsening in five of the six Latin American countries it surveyed, with Mexicans now viewing China more favorably 59 percent to 40. Tellingly, large majorities in all six say it is Washington, not Beijing, that interferes in other countries’ affairs. China says that it has an explicitly “non-interventionist” foreign policy in Latin America.

A South American diplomat speaking on condition of anonymity said that “if the U.S. really wants to compete, then they need to offer alternatives. Right now, all they are offering is force. That doesn’t build anything for anyone. We need to develop.”

Since President Donald Trump’s return to office in early 2025, drug conflicts in Latin America have ramped up, and drug trafficking has been increasing, with global cocaine production at an all-time high as per 2026 data. Ecuador, one of Trump’s closest allies, closed 2025 with more than 9,200 homicides, the deadliest year in its modern history.

Meanwhile, where Ecuador has seen real progress, it has been with China. Under a free trade agreement in force since 2024, Ecuador’s exports to China grew 23 percent in the first half of 2026, and its economy minister expects China to overtake the U.S. as the country’s top trading partner “within a matter of months.”

Nowhere perhaps is this divergence more apparent than in Venezuela. Since U.S. forces captured President Nicolás Maduro in January, the country has been openly described, including by TIME, as a de facto “vassal state” of Washington. Yet acting President Delcy Rodríguez thanked Beijing for condemning the operation, and her government has since reaffirmed its support for the One China principle amid cross-strait tensions. Chinese oil ventures were still pumping an estimated 164,000 barrels per day as of August, and China was Venezuela’s largest trading partner from 2019 through 2025.

Regionally, China-Latin America trade hit a record $565 billion in 2025, up from roughly $12 billion in 2000. China has been South America’s top trading partner since 2015, maintains currency swap and settlement arrangements with Brazil and Argentina, and saw 22 of the region’s 33 countries sign on to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

The U.S. push to force Latin American countries out of the BRI has had almost no success, with Panama the only successful case. Even the U.S. military’s publication Diálogo Américas notes that 21 nations remain members. Still, Panama continues to recognize Beijing over Taipei, has a Chinese state-owned consortium building its $2.6 billion Fourth Bridge over the canal, which is now 37 percent complete, and grew its exports to China by roughly 40 percent in 2025.

With this leverage, China has still been outspoken on certain geopolitical dynamics. Beijing condemned the Venezuela operation as a “blatant use of force,” and has repeatedly demanded an end to the U.S. blockade of Cuba, accusing Washington of using “invented allegations” to justify it. Regionally, these are framed as defending local sovereignty, rather than interference.

The contrast extends to the Amazon. Washington has paired a push for the region’s critical minerals with an expanded military footprint, making the rainforest another front in the war on drugs. China has instead financed manufacturing and ports, and funded the first inter-Amazonian highway, from BYD’s $1 billion plant in Bahia to Chancay. It has also endorsed Brazil’s Tropical Forests Forever Facility, which reserves a fifth of its payouts for Indigenous and local communities, supporting development with those communities rather than against them.

With President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva winning a fourth presidential term on October 25, and the BRICS bloc more empowered than ever, with former Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff re-elected to lead its New Development Bank through 2030 and touting billions in new financing, it is clear this approach toward development will continue in at least the near future. On its current trajectory, the U.S. risks excluding itself from that development, and thus, from Latin America’s future.

All of this shows that soft power is still king in Latin America, no matter how much force Washington wants to use. In the end, force can even become counterproductive. Treating Latin American states as subordinates rather than equal partners may prove to be a grave error for Washington’s plans for “regional hegemony.” As Lula told Xi Jinping in Beijing, “no one is going to prohibit Brazil from improving its relationship with China.”
